title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 20
paragraphs: The infantry regiments that had been caught off guard at the edge of the woods came pouring out of the trees, companies jumbled together, retreating as a disorganized mob. One soldier, in his terror, let out the senseless cry "Cut off!"—those words that are so devastating in battle—and that single shout infected the entire crowd with panic.
"Surrounded! Cut off! We're done for!" screamed the men as they fled.

The instant he heard the gunfire and the shouts behind him, the general realized something terrible had happened to his regiment. The thought that he—a model officer with decades of unblemished service—might be held responsible at headquarters for negligence or incompetence hit him so hard that he forgot about the obstinate cavalry colonel, forgot his own dignity as a general, and above all forgot any concern for his personal safety. He grabbed the back of his saddle, spurred his horse, and galloped toward his regiment through a storm of bullets that flew all around him but, by some miracle, missed. His one desire was to find out what had happened and, at any cost, fix whatever had gone wrong—so that he, a model officer of twenty-two years' service who had never once been reprimanded, would not be blamed.

Having galloped safely through the French lines, he reached a field behind the copse, across which his men were streaming in all directions, running downhill in defiance of every order. The decisive moment of moral crisis—the kind that determines the outcome of battles—had arrived. Would this panicked mob of soldiers respond to their commander's voice, or would they ignore him and keep running? Despite his desperate shouting—the kind that used to terrify his soldiers—despite his furious, purple face, distorted beyond recognition, despite the wild flourishing of his saber, the soldiers kept running, talking, firing into the air, and refusing to obey. The moral crisis was tipping unmistakably toward a rout.

The general had a coughing fit from all the shouting and the powder smoke and stopped in despair. Everything seemed lost. But at that moment, the attacking French suddenly and inexplicably turned and ran back, disappearing from the edge of the woods. Russian sharpshooters appeared in the copse. It was Timokhin's company—the only unit that had held together in the forest. They'd been lying in ambush in a ditch and now burst upon the French from behind. Timokhin, armed with nothing but a sword, had charged the enemy with such a wild cry and such furious, almost crazed determination that the stunned French had dropped their muskets and fled. Dolokhov, running alongside Timokhin, killed a Frenchman at point-blank range and was the first to seize a surrendering French officer by the collar. The Russian fugitives turned around. The battalions reformed. The French, who had come within an inch of splitting the left flank in two, were beaten back for the moment. The reserve units linked up again, and the fighting came to an end. The regimental commander and Major Ekonomov had halted by a bridge to let the retreating companies file past when a soldier walked up and grabbed the commander's stirrup, practically leaning against him. The man wore a bluish broadcloth coat, had no pack or cap, his head was bandaged, and a French ammunition pouch hung from his shoulder. He held an officer's sword in his hand. The soldier was pale, his blue eyes stared insolently into the commander's face, and his lips were set in a smile. Though the commander was busy giving instructions to Major Ekonomov, he couldn't help noticing the man.

"Your excellency, two trophies," said Dolokhov, pointing to the French sword and pouch. "I took an officer prisoner. I stopped the company from retreating." He was breathing hard from exhaustion and spoke in short, clipped sentences. "The entire company can confirm it. Please remember this, your excellency."
"All right, all right," the commander replied, and turned back to Major Ekonomov.
But Dolokhov didn't leave. He untied the handkerchief around his head, pulled it off, and showed the blood matted in his hair.
"A bayonet wound. I stayed at the front. Remember, your excellency."

Tushin's battery had been entirely forgotten, and only at the very end of the battle did Prince Bagration, still hearing cannon fire from the center, send his orderly staff officer—and later Prince Andrew as well—to order the battery to pull back as quickly as possible. When the infantry support assigned to Tushin's battery had been moved away mid-battle by someone's order, the battery had simply kept firing. The only reason it wasn't overrun by the French was that the enemy couldn't imagine anyone would have the audacity to keep firing from four completely undefended guns. On the contrary, the sheer aggressiveness of this battery led the French to believe that the main Russian forces were concentrated here, in the center. Twice they'd tried to storm the position, and both times they'd been driven back by grapeshot from four lonely guns on the hilltop.
Shortly after Bagration had left, Tushin managed to set fire to Schon Grabern.
"Look at them scramble! It's burning! Look at the smoke! Magnificent! Look at the smoke, the smoke!" the artillerymen exclaimed, their spirits soaring.

All the guns, without waiting for orders, opened fire toward the blaze. Egging each other on, the soldiers shouted with every shot: "Beautiful! That's the stuff! Look at that! Magnificent!" The fire, fanned by the breeze, was spreading fast. The French columns that had advanced past the village fell back. But as if in retaliation, the enemy brought up ten guns to the right of the village and began shelling Tushin's battery.

In their childlike excitement over the fire and their success in bombarding the French, the artillerymen didn't even notice this new battery until two balls, and then four more, crashed among their guns—one toppling two horses and another ripping off a wagon driver's leg. But their high spirits weren't dampened, only redirected. The dead horses were replaced from a reserve gun carriage, the wounded were carried away, and all four guns were turned against the ten-gun battery. Tushin's fellow officer had been killed at the start of the engagement, and within an hour seventeen of the forty men in the gun crews had been put out of action. But the artillerymen were as spirited and lively as ever. Twice they spotted French infantry approaching from below and blasted them with grapeshot.

Little Tushin, moving about weakly and awkwardly, kept telling his orderly, "Refill my pipe for that one!" and then, scattering sparks, ran forward shielding his eyes with his small hand to peer at the French.
"Give it to 'em, lads!" he kept saying, grabbing the gun wheels himself and working the elevation screws.

Through the smoke, deafened by the constant explosions that made him flinch every time, Tushin ran from gun to gun without ever taking his pipe from his mouth—now aiming, now counting charges, now shouting orders about replacing dead or wounded horses and hitching fresh ones, calling out in his thin, high-pitched, wavering voice. His face grew more and more animated. Only when a man was killed or wounded did he wince and turn away from the sight, shouting angrily at the soldiers who, as always happens, hesitated about carrying off the dead and injured. The soldiers—mostly big, handsome men, as is typical in artillery companies, a head taller and twice as broad as their little officer—watched their commander the way children watch a grown-up in an awkward situation. Whatever expression crossed his face was instantly mirrored on theirs.

Thanks to the overwhelming noise and the demands of constant action, Tushin felt not the slightest trace of fear. The thought that he might be killed or badly wounded never once entered his mind. On the contrary, he grew more and more exhilarated. It felt to him as though an enormously long time had passed—nearly a full day—since he'd first spotted the enemy and fired that opening shot, and that the patch of ground he was standing on was a place he'd known for years. Although he was thinking of everything, weighing everything, doing everything that the best officer in his situation could possibly do, he was in a state closer to feverish delirium or intoxication.

From the deafening roar of his own guns around him, the whistle and thud of enemy cannonballs, the flushed and sweating faces of his crew bustling around the guns, the sight of blood—human and horse—the small puffs of smoke on the enemy's hill (each one followed inevitably by a ball that flew past and struck the ground, a man, a gun, a horse)—from all of this, a fantastical world of his own making had taken hold of his mind and was, at that moment, giving him pleasure. The enemy's cannon were not guns in his imagination but pipes, from which an invisible smoker occasionally blew puffs of smoke.
"There... he's puffing again," Tushin muttered to himself as a small cloud rose from the hill and drifted in a streak to the left on the wind.
"Now watch for the ball... we'll toss it right back."
"What did you say, your honor?" asked an artilleryman standing close by, who'd heard him muttering.
"Nothing... just a shell," he answered.

"Come on, Matvevna old girl!" he said to himself. "Matvevna" was the pet name his imagination had given to the farthest gun in the battery—a large, old-fashioned piece. The French swarming around their guns looked to him like ants. In this fantasy world of his, the handsome drunk who was Number One on the second gun's crew had become "uncle"; Tushin watched him more than anyone else and took delight in his every movement. The sound of musket fire at the foot of the hill, rising and falling, seemed to him like someone breathing. He listened carefully to the ebb and flow of those sounds.
"Daughter of Matthew" was the literal meaning of the name.
"Ah, breathing again, breathing!" he muttered to himself.
He pictured himself as an enormously tall, powerful man hurling cannonballs at the French with both hands.
"Come on now, Matvevna, old girl, don't let me down!" he was saying as he moved away from the gun, when a strange, unfamiliar voice called out above his head: "Captain Tushin! Captain!"
Tushin spun around, startled. It was the staff officer who had kicked him out of the booth at Grunth. The man was shouting in a breathless, gasping voice:
"Are you out of your mind? You've been ordered to retreat twice, and you..."
"Why do they have it in for me?" thought Tushin, looking up at his superior in alarm.
"I... it's not..." he stammered, raising two fingers to his cap. "I..."

But the staff officer never finished what he was saying. A cannonball whizzed so close that he ducked and folded over his horse's neck. He started to speak again, but another ball cut him short. He yanked his horse around and galloped away.
"Retreat! Everyone retreat!" he shouted from a distance.
The soldiers laughed. A moment later, another adjutant arrived with the same order.

It was Prince Andrew. The first thing he saw as he rode up to where Tushin's guns were positioned was a horse with a broken leg, unharnessed, lying beside the harnessed horses and screaming pitifully. Blood gushed from its leg like water from a spring. Among the limbers lay several dead men. One cannonball after another flew overhead as he approached, and he felt a shudder run down his spine. But the mere thought of being afraid snapped him out of it. "I cannot be afraid," he thought, and dismounted slowly among the guns. He delivered the order but did not leave the battery. He decided to stay and oversee the removal of the guns himself. Together with Tushin, stepping over the bodies and under withering French fire, he supervised the withdrawal of the cannons.
"There was a staff officer here a minute ago, but he bolted," an artilleryman said to Prince Andrew. "Not like your honor."

Prince Andrew said nothing to Tushin. They were both too absorbed in the work to seem to notice each other. When they'd managed to limber up the only two undamaged guns out of the original four and began moving downhill—leaving behind one shattered cannon and one unicorn—Prince Andrew rode up to Tushin.
"Well then, until we meet again..." he said, holding out his hand.
"Goodbye, my dear fellow," said Tushin. "Dear soul! Goodbye, my dear fellow!" And for some reason he couldn't explain, tears suddenly filled his eyes.
